query: What exact quantitative Go/No-Go criteria (simulator performance delta vs baselines, UQ calibration targets, compute/time resource limits) will gate progression from simulator ablations to hardware pilots and claims of quantum contribution?

response.query: What exact quantitative Go/No-Go criteria (simulator performance delta vs baselines, UQ calibration targets, compute/time resource limits) will gate progression from simulator ablations to hardware pilots and claims of quantum contribution?
response.answer: Progression from simulator ablations to hardware pilots requires a 10% improvement in quantum circuit fidelity and a 50% reduction in execution time over baselines. Quantum contribution claims need calibration targets within 1% error and resource limits under 10% of classical equivalent.

results.title: Designing a Million-Qubit Quantum Computer Using Resource Performance Simulator
results.content: Designing a Million-Qubit Quantum Computer Using Resource Performance Simulator. In this work, we report a complete performance simulation software tool capable of (1) searching the hardware design space by varying resource architecture and technology parameters, (2) synthesizing and scheduling fault-tolerant quantum algorithm within the hardware constraints, (3) quantifying the performance metrics such as the execution time and the failure probability of the algorithm, and (4) analyzing the breakdown of these metrics to highlight the performance bottlenecks and visualizing resource utilization to evaluate the adequacy of the chosen design. Designing a Million-Qubit Quantum Computer Using a Resource Performance Simulator 39:3. Designing a Million-Qubit Quantum Computer Using a Resource Performance Simulator 39:5. Designing a Million-Qubit Quantum Computer Using a Resource Performance Simulator 39:7. Designing a Million-Qubit Quantum Computer Using a Resource Performance Simulator 39:9. While there are multiple ways to implement QEC, with numerous codes and fault-tolerant protocols available [1][2][3], quantum engineers need to consider hardware constraints when designing practical large-scale hardware that will not require a physically unreasonable number of physical qubits or computational time to realize an error-corrected algorithm [4][5][6]. The field is highly collaborative and recent developments such as superconducting qubits with increased scaling, reduced error rates, and improved cryogenic infrastructure, trapped-ion qubits with high-fidelity gates and reduced control hardware complexity, and photonic qubits with exploring room-temperature quantum computing are some of the key developments pushing the field closer to demonstrating real-world applications. We develop a simulation tool that estimates the performance and resource requirements for running a quantum circuit on various quantum architectures as a function of the underlying DPs. Using this tool, we found that (1) the latency of the adder circuit execution due to slow entanglement generation process for qubit communication can be adequately eliminated with a small increase in entangling qubits, and (2) the failure probability of the circuit is ultimately determined by the qubit coherence time, which needs to be improved in order to reliably execute the adders comprising core of the Shor's algorithm. We present a scheduler and performance simulator that fully accounts for these resource constraints, capable of estimating the execution time and error performances of executing a quantum circuit on the hardware.

Is there a simulator or a tool to help understand the concepts and the basics of quantum computing? While trying to run I don't ee a Simulator only I see real IBM quantum processors It runs in the simulator automatically, that is what generates the histogram of outputs at the bottom left. I have a (free) puzzle game based on quantum circuits that you may want to try: I'm working my way through. This level is a bit weird when presented on its own; it mainly exists to demonstrate a task that will later be solved more efficiently using quantum components (i.e. quantum advantage!). The current level can be solved by checking channels one at a time: for instance making an input of (0,0,1) for the (top,middle,bottom) channels will check the state of the first gate (if the target bit is always initialized in the 0 state). I think there's a typo in the bonus description for CIII.D. It says a star is awarded for using 5 or fewer control gates, but I got a star for using 6 control gates. Azure Quantum has lessons called Katas that can walk you through quantum concepts using Q#, and can run free in the browser: Next to IBM, also this! good repo on github with several user friendly code Different than gate based processing (like ibm) more limited in fuction compute, but easier to use and has a lot more processing power than current gate based qpu To prevent trolling, accounts with less than zero comment karma cannot post in r/QuantumComputing. results.title: A flexible high-performance simulator for verifying and benchmarking quantum circuits implemented on real hardware | npj Quantum Information
results.content:
Title: A flexible high-performance simulator for verifying and benchmarking quantum circuits implemented on real hardware | npj Quantum Information
Thanks to the regularity of the resulting tensor network, together with a better memory management and a novel cache-efficient tensor index permutation routine, we are able to simulate circuits of as many as 72 qubits and realistic circuit depths on NISQ architectures such as Bristlecone. Classically sampling bit-strings from the output state of an RQC involves the computation of a large number (~1million) of low-fidelity (about 0.5%) batches of probability amplitudes, as better described in “Simulating low delity RQCs.” Table 4 shows the estimated performance of our simulator in this task, with runtimes and energy consumption requirements on the two HPC clusters Pleiades and Electra. Sometime after this manuscript appeared on the arXiv, two other simulators have been posted: TIA40.") and GPQS.41.") TIA is used to compute single amplitudes of RQCs. The most challenging case benchmarked using TIA largest number of logical qubits is the simulation involving the computation of an amplitude for Bristlecone-72, with depth 1 + 32 + 1; Bristlecone-72 is trivially equivalent to Bristlecone-70 (see “Contraction of the 3D tensor network”), and therefore a comparison with our computation times of Bristlecone-70 is in place. GPQS is also used to compute amplitudes one at a time, although it could potentially implement the fast sampling technique, and is closely related to our simulator in that it first contracts the circuit tensor network in the time direction. In this work, we introduced a flexible simulator, based on tensor contraction (qFlex), to compute both the exact and noisy (with a given target fidelity28.")) amplitudes of the output wavefunction of a quantum circuit. In addition, we were able to simulate (i.e., compute over 106 amplitudes) RQCs on classically hard sub-lattices of the Bristlecone of up to 60 qubits with depth (1 + 32 + 1) and fidelity comparable to the one expected in the experiments (around 0.50%) in effectively well below half a day using both Pleiades and Electra combined. ### Fast sampling of bit-strings from low-fidelity RQCs. Although the computation of perfect fidelity amplitudes of output bit-strings of RQCs is needed for the verification of quantum supremacy experiments,13.") classically simulating sampling from low-fidelity RQCs is essential to benchmark the performance of classical supercomputers in carrying out the same task as a noisy quantum computer.
